next.name: MageCart
next.headline: MageCart: card-skimming crews that plant code on online shops
next.in_short: MageCart is a name for hackers who steal payment card numbers from online stores. Reports describe attacks on single shops, cloud-hosted platforms and tag-manager scripts.

sentences.t: MageCart is listed in the MISP galaxy catalogue as a threat actor, with no aliases or tools recorded there.
WIRED describes Magecart as a group of hackers that steals credit card numbers, often by skimming card data from ecommerce sites.
Malwarebytes refers to the criminal part of the Magecart "cabal", which suggests the name covers more than one operator.
The focus is online shopping. WIRED says the hackers cast the widest possible net to find vulnerable ecommerce sites.
Malwarebytes describes compromised shopping sites that were injected with a single line of code loading a remote script.
A report on the Volusion breach says most Magecart attacks happen when hackers use vulnerabilities in self-hosted stores to plant skimmer code.
The core technique is web card skimming. Malicious code on a shop page captures card details that shoppers type in.
Malwarebytes found skimmers that overlay a fake payment frame on the real payment form and send the stolen data back in encoded form.
The same report says the crooks registered free Heroku accounts to host skimmer infrastructure. Malwarebytes had earlier documented skimmers served from GitHub and Amazon S3 buckets.
Sucuri describes the ATMZOW skimmer, which is planted through Google Tag Manager containers. It used heavy obfuscation and 40 newly registered domains, many hidden behind a firewall.
Sucuri says Google removed one container, and the actors created new ones and reinfected sites. Sucuri also says Group IB linked this skimmer to a 2015 infection that hit thousands of Magento sites.
WIRED, in July 2019, said Magecart had been behind some of the bigger hacks of recent years, from British Airways to Ticketmaster.
WIRED reported the group had hit 17,000 domains in a few months, helped by poor security hygiene. The author warned the method could lead to even bigger problems.
In October 2019 hackers breached Volusion, a provider of cloud-hosted online stores. The report says more than 6,500 stores were affected and the number could be higher.
The report calls the Volusion case a Magecart-style supply-chain attack. It says seven service providers were breached earlier that year through misconfigured cloud-hosting accounts.
Malwarebytes reported the Heroku-hosted skimmers to Heroku, and the abusive instances were taken down. It said it would likely keep seeing skimmers abuse more cloud services.
Shop owners should treat unexpected scripts on their pages as a sign of compromise, as Sucuri advises.
Keep store software patched and review who can change your cloud and tag-manager accounts.
